<description>
{
 "summary": "Move compiler and linker hardening flags into a dedicated `hardening_interface` CMake library linked by `core_interface`, and propagate supported hardening flags to the secp256k1 subtree. A new CMake helper validates the hardening flags against the C compiler before passing them to secp256k1.",
 "problem": "The secp256k1 subtree does not use `core_interface`, leaving its objects built without hardening flags (such as `_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, `-fstack-protector-all`, `-fstack-clash-protection`, and branch/control-flow protection) unless enabled by compiler defaults. Because modern linkers require every linked object file to contain control-flow properties before tagging the final binary, unhardened secp256k1 objects cause final executables like `bitcoind` to completely lose hardware control-flow markers (e.g. AArch64 BTI/PAC/GCS or x86_64 CET).",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'On aarch64 Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15, the three secp256k1 objects are the only ones in the build tree without the control flow property, so master's bitcoind has no AArch64 feature note... The same build then shows AArch64 feature: BTI, PAC, GCS on bitcoind.'",
  "Linked issues/PRs #30677 and #30685 track control-flow capabilities for release binaries."
 ],

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.
